articles.headline: MEDORA.
articles.text:
Now that the era of prosperity is fairly inaugurated, Medora is destined for some time to be the liveliest town on the Northern Pacific. Numerous buildings are in contemplation, many of them, however, waiting for the brick which will soon be manufactured here in large quantities. The present season is not the time when the Hills merchants receive the most freight, but large quantities will be handled from here all summer. As the Northern Pacific doubles freight rates Nov. 1, the busiest season will be from Oct. 1 clear on into the winter, a vast quantity being shipped to arrive here before Nov. 1. The freight-house will be begun soon and the Marquis will probably build it of brick. Besides putting in an additional side-track the railroad company will make many other improvements. City lots are going off rapidly, eight being sold yesterday.

The best part of our growth is that there is no boom in connection with it. It is all legitimate growth. From its site alone, Medora was destined to be a good-sized town. As it would have been a cattle town, it would probably have been the richest for its size in Dakota. Then came the Marquis de Mores, establishing the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co., the largest thing of its kind in the world. This would also, of itself, make a good town, as many industries are bound to spring up therefrom. Now comes the freight, stage and mail routes of which we have the complete control. Not a pound of freight will be shipped from any point on the Northern Pacific R. R. except from Medora. The stage route will be in full operation as soon as stages and horses can be procured and the mail route will be established as soon as an appropriation passes congress. Less than these three made Bismarck so successful for a time with ten dollars to where there is one there now. Consequently, if analogy goes to show anything, we will have a better town than was Bismarck in the heyday of its prosperity. In addition to all this, there is almost a certainty that inside of a year a railroad will be completed between Medora and the Hills. It can be built at less than an average of $5,000 a mile and will be a paying institution from the send-off. It will make the whole southern Bad Lands and the Black Hills country tributary to Medora and make probably the largest city in the territory. These are facts, not fancies, and all our conclusions are logical deductions which are proved by ample experience.

Medora is assuredly the coming town of Dakota.
articles.summary: Editorial predicting Medora's growth on brick-making, the Marquis de Mores' refrigerator car company, control of the Black Hills freight, stage and mail routes, and a planned Medora–Black Hills railroad; eight city lots sold yesterday.

articles.headline: BOOMING.
articles.text:
We wish all the emigrants who are passing through Dakota at the rate of from three to five hundred a day, bound for Washington and Oregon, could speak with returning emigrants who are coming back at the rate of two to three hundred a day. Monday morning, for instance, there were about two hundred and fifty emigrants on the train returning east, and a more disgusted lot of people it has never been our lot to see. They were all returning from Washington, Oregon and the Cœur D'Alene mines, where they had been lured by circulars stating that there was plenty of work for all and fortunes were waiting every arrival.

The amount of the matter is that in all those places it is harder for a laboring man to get a job than it is in overcrowed New York and Chicago. Of course, the reports of the returning emigrants are rather highly colored, but they report that there are thousands there who do not know where their next meal is to come from. These reports will be scattered all over the east and do incalculable damage to the west.

The moral of this whole matter is that for a temporary success the railroads and town-site owners are killing the goose which would in the future lay the golden eggs. If we could makee very one in the east know that "booming" is almost a synonym for lying we think it would be an immense benefit to this whole country. What a useless and wholly damnable scheme the lying circulars are, a little thought will show to any one. We have never seen one yet that did not enlarge the facts far beyond what they warrant. They are all issued for the purpose of inducing settlers and speculators to invest. Suppose, as is generally the case, that they are successful in their aim. Settlers come and find nothing more than they could find in fifty other places. Will any reasonable man claim that this is legitimate, or in the end, profitable way in which to gain citizens? If there is such a man, let him go to any eastern-bound train and interview the emigrants. We must again quote the statement of our Dickinson correspondent: "The simple truth about this country, when it becomes known, will bring men and means to develop it quite as rapidly as is consistent with a healthy growth."

The reader may notice that our remarks have been directed to points far west from here and think they do not apply to Dakota. We have taken the far west because the emigrants we have seen are returning from there and because the swindle is greater as they have to pay more to get there. The whole of Dakota is and has been cursed with a set of men who make "booming" their livelihood. Every settler who is misled by their false statements should be able to and we think can sue and recover damages. A boomer is a liar every time. If a man comes to Dakota with enough money to get a start and a willingness to work as hard as he would east, he can do no better than to come. There are fortunes for that kind of men. For men who expect to make money easier here than they could in the east we have no use. They are a clog on the rest and are the class of easily discouraged men who do far more harm than good. Happy Dakota and happy west when the boomer is no more in the land!
articles.summary: Editorial attacking land 'booming' circulars, citing some 250 disgusted emigrants seen returning east on Monday's train from Washington, Oregon and the Coeur d'Alene mines.

articles.headline: A Twenty-Six Hours' Run.
articles.text:
The Marquis de Mores and Jos. Pennell returned yesterday morning from their Deadwood trip. From the Black Hills papers and interviews it is very manifest that the trip was a great success. They started a week ago yesterday morning and made the trip in forty-eight hours, passing on the road Messrs. Allen and Jones who had thirty-five hours the start.

According to Mr. Pennell they had a parrot and monkey kind of a time on the way down. They were caught on the open ridge in a driving storm of snow and rain without even a blanket to cover them and for six hours were compelled to walk around their horses to keep alive. Their only protection from the storm was their saddle blankets thrown over their heads. Between Spearfish and Deadwood they were met by a delegation of the principal citizens of Deadwood and there was a perfect ovation. The principal mines and points of interest were visited and everywhere the party met with an enthusiastic reception. Several banquets were given, and aside from the business done, many warm friends were made.

The return trip was made in much better time. Starting Monday they arrived here yesterday morning, being in the saddle just twenty-six hours. This fact alone prevents all argument as to the "practicability" of our route. If any one doubts it, there is $500 to $10,000 here that says the trip can be made in twenty-four hours. That is, in twenty-four hours after leaving Medora the rider will be in Deadwood.

The merchants of the Hills to a man are interested in our route and there is now no doubt that every pound of Black Hills freight will be shipped via Medora. At a meeting of the Black Hills Shippers' Association it was decided to send all freight by our line and a telegram was sent to Keyes & Bramble to that effect and offering them the position of forwarders. Mr. Keyes went through here Tuesday evening and reported their acceptance of the offer and that there were 40,000 pounds of freight at Belfield that would be shipped here immediately. In addition to this, Marquis has agreed to put on a tri-weekly line of stages, which will be running as soon as the stages can be procured. The railroad is perfectly feasible and before fall it is expected that at least fifty miles will be built.

The route itself is even better than was reported. It is thought, that if anything, to be under 180 miles and of this 150 miles is absolutely devoid of gumbo. For the remaining thirty miles it only appears in places and will be no trouble except when the frost is coming out of the ground in the spring. At this season there will be very little freighting so that the gumbo question is not worth consideration.

The route has now repeatedly been pronounced one of the best, if not the best, in the country and there seems no doubt on the subject.

We don't believe in kicking a man when he is down and we hope our citizens will join with us in dropping a tear to the ephemeral dreams of freight routes held by some of Medora's suburbs down the road.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Mores and Joseph Pennell returned from a ride to Deadwood, making the return in 26 hours; the Black Hills Shippers' Association chose the Medora route, with Keyes & Bramble as forwarders, and the Marquis agreed to run a tri-weekly stage line.

articles.text: It was deemed best by many interested to put off the organization of the Bad Lands stock association till next fall. Several reasons led to this result, among them the following: That there is no business of immediate importance to come before the meeting; that at the present season it is impossible for all interested to attend a meeting, many of them being away, and finally that the subject has not received as thorough a canvass as it should have. Altogether it seems better to put off the organization, as a poor association is little better than none at all and will prevent the establishment of a good one. It is also better to wait for the reason that we can draw members as far as the Black Hills, and very soon a steel highway will afford ready access to Medora for all Hills stockmen. It is merely putting off the day for the purpose of forming a far more important organization.
articles.summary: Organization of the Bad Lands stock association is postponed until fall.

articles.headline: DICKINSON NOTES.
articles.text:
DICKINSON, April 23, 1884.

In spite of frosty mornings our farmers are rushing seed into the ground and before the next issue there will be several hundred acres sown here. The ground is reported to be in first-class condition and prospects are bright for good harvests.

The county convention select Mr. Campbell to represent the Republicans at the territorial convention to select delegates to the national convention at Chicago.

About 2,000 head of young stock cattle passed through en route for Montana Saturday and Sunday. The manager reported serious losses resulting from inadequate accommodations at feeding stations along the N. P. There are over one hundred car-loads yet to come on. The cattle were nearly all yearlings and none were more than two-year-olds.

Editor Scott, of The Press, has betaken himself to the old Ohio scenes for a brief season.

Freight continues to arrive for the Black Hills and is forwarded as rapidly as it comes.

ANTHROPOS.
articles.summary: Dickinson correspondence: spring seeding, Mr. Campbell chosen for the Republican territorial convention, 2,000 young cattle passing west to Montana, Editor Scott of the Press gone to Ohio, Black Hills freight moving.

articles.headline: Coming Sure.
articles.text: D. A. McPherson, cashier of the First National bank of this city, is a man who is silent on all subjects unless he has something to say, and he now speaks to the point: "The Northern Pacific will extend fifty miles of their line from Medora toward the Black Hills this summer." The above statement was made in public on Wednesday evening last. The Pioneer made the statement over a week ago that the signs of the times pointed to the building of the portion of a line from the above point, and that T. G. Jones had gone to the headquarters of the company to bid on the work of grading. These threads followed up lead to the discovery of facts, which will eventually be of great benefit to this country. It is sufficient to state that the lea[ven?] is working, and in less than sixty days we shall see developments that will confirm all rumors. It is now almost a settled conclusion that the reseravtion will not be opened at this session of congress and the granting of the right of way to the Milwaukee & St. Paul and Chicago & Northwestern railways may be delayed. Therefore, a movement by the Northern Pacific to capture the trade of this country is opportune and will be pushed with all possible vigor. Before snow flies next winter we may take a hack to the terminus of the Medora and Black Hills railroad. It is not a fanciful dream, but an easy project that can be accomplished with the assurance of a paying business from its completion.—[Black Hills Pioneer.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Black Hills Pioneer: Deadwood banker D. A. McPherson says the Northern Pacific will build fifty miles of line from Medora toward the Black Hills this summer.

articles.headline: STOCK NOTES.
articles.text:
Beckwith & Quinn, ranchmen from Western Wyoming, branded 90 per cent. of calves last year and there were no mavericks in the count. How high is this?

Telegraphic reports from Austin, Tex., say that a cattle syndicate is negotiating for the 3,000,000 acres of land in the Panhandle of Texas, known as the capital lands.

Renewed confidence in the outlook is everywhere manifest among stockmen as the news from the outlying ranges comes in. The losses are reported small and cattle generally in fair condition.—[Cheyenne Live Stock Journal.

Reports from Nevada, Idaho, Montana and Dakota as to the range cattle are very flattering. In Oregon, Washington Territory and Utah, cattle as a rule have done well, but in a few small areas considerable loss has been sustained on account of deep snow.

All kinds of stock are very weak at this time and when they get into soft ground many die from dampness, getting mired down and unable to get out. A great many cattle will die within the next two weeks, as there is just enough green grass to weaken them and when once down a large per cent never get up.—[Cheyenne Transporter.

The Dominion Cattle Company, which has now nearly 97,000 cattle on 284,000 acres of the Cherokee Reservation, which is leased for two cents an acre from the United States government, has thus far proved a decided success. Last year its capital stock, amounting to almost $250,000, brought a net profit of $100,000 out of which a dividend of 20 per cent has been declared.—[Texas Stockman.

The different associations, composed of owners of cattle on the western and southwestern ranges, have within the past six weeks held their annual meetings and from these meetings a general idea can be obtained as to the feeling existing among cattte owners. The business of these associations have been conducted in a systematic member, and no loop-hole left unguarded by which the interests of the members may be infringed upon. The attendance at these meetings has been unusually large, showing the interest taken by the members. This, however, is hardly to be remarked upon, from the fact that among range cattle owners there is a community of interest which they cannot fail to appreciate without affecting the value of their property. The Colorado Cattle Growers' Association was the first of the kind in the west and from it has grown these other associations, which have been found by those interested to be a necessity. The amount of capital represented at these different meetings is large and the investment having been made in many cases by capitalists whose interests are entrusted to others, causes the business to assnme a position quite different from what it was five or six years ago. Now the investment is made upon a basis from which certain returns are expected, whereas six, ten or fifteen years ago there was a speculative character in the ownership of range cattle which does not exist at the present day. Now there are breeding ranches and steer ranches, and the conclusion is arrived at that to raise cattle in the south and let them mature in the north is the proper way in which to conduct the business of raising cattle on the range. The reports as to the manner in which the cattle passed through the winter are to the effect that with the exception of one or two localities the losses have been light. The calf crop promises to be fair and upon this question we have a few words. It is false economy to buy less than one bull to every twenty-five cows, or to give the preference to yearling bulls, when they should be guaranteed yearlings, or two-year-olds. There is one question upon which range cattle owners appear to be unanimous and that is in endeavoring to protect their herds from contagious diseases. They realize the importance of avoiding the appearance of a contagious disease which would be ruinous in its effects. The outlook for the prices of range cattle the coming summer is not discouraging, but at the same time the expectation of inflated prices should not be encouraged.—[Live Stock Indicator.

One of the striking developments of the cattle business in the west in the last few years has been the wonderful increase in the value of female stock. In the earlier days of ranching, when stockers could be obtained with ease from sources which then seemed inexhaustible, cows were considered of little value. Indeed, no more than three or four years ago they were a drug in the frontier market. But with the giving out of stocker supplies in Oregon, Montana and elsewhere, ranchmen began to see that they must raise their own stockers and cows commenced straightway to increase in value. No longer ago than in 1880 purchasers of ranch property often attempted to throw the cows aside altogether and if they were taken into the trade at all it was at a paltry figure. It was considered quite a good thing in those days to get from $20 to $25 straight through for a herd of good cows, with calves thrown in without valuation. For two or three years past, however, the stock has been in increased request and corresponding scarcity, until now, [in the?] northwest, prices range from $35 to $[illegible], according to locality and quality, with a supply insufficient for the demand. The limit of prices will, of course, be reached when cows can be taken out freely from the states at the same figures. It will only be a matter of a short time, too, until the demand for cows for ranching purposes will be as great in the states lying along the Missouri river as it now is for stockers in the same region—[National Stockman.
articles.summary: Stock Notes column of range news, mostly clipped from western stock journals: branding percentages, a Texas Panhandle land syndicate, winter losses, the Dominion Cattle Company, stock-association meetings and rising cow prices.

articles.text: A piece of the clay that will be used for the brick was molded slightly by hand and left in the sun to dry for several hours. At the end of that time it was almost as hard as a stone, much harder for instance than the Sims pressed brick. The piece is now in our office where it can be seen by visitors. There is no doubt whatever that sun-dried brick could be used successfully. The price is so low though that it is hardly worth while to try the experiment.
articles.summary: A sun-dried sample of Medora brick clay is on display at the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: A great commotion was stirred up last Saturday by the report that thirteen horses and mules had been stolen. A man named Martin had followed the trail several miles and then returned. A party was immediately made up, consisting of Messrs. Paddock, Roberts, Jolly, Packard and Martin, to go in pursuit. Preparations were made to follow the thieves a month if necessary, and the pursuing party certainly meant business as all but Roberts and Martin had stock missing. The pursuit came to a successful but rather ludicrous termination by running across all the stock about seven miles from town. Whether they were driven there or simply wandered off is still a question.
articles.summary: A posse including Paddock, Roberts, Jolly, Packard and Martin chased supposedly stolen horses and mules, found grazing seven miles out.

articles.text: Peter Book and family arrived last Saturday, together with five experienced brick-makers. Lumber was bought immediately and work begun on the grounds, which are located south of town where the Deadwood trail separates from the river. Two machines and all the implements necessary are on the ground and the work of clearing and digging wells is going rapidly forward. Mr. Book is enthusiastic over the clay, stating it to the best he has ever seen. The same view is taken of it by all the men. The first kiln will be done in less than three weeks. Several kinds of clay will be used so as to find out as much as possible about the varieties abounding here. There will be a number of brick buildings erected as soon as the brick is ready and we will soon have a city of which to be proud. The brick work could not possibly be in better hands, as Mr. Book is an experienced contractor and builder as well as a brick-maker.
articles.summary: Brick-maker Peter Book arrived with family and five brick-makers and began a brickyard south of town.

articles.summary: Mr. Bramble is in town preparing to ship freight via Medora.

articles.text: Howard Eaton has made application for a policy of insurance for the Custer Trail ranch property. It is an example that should be universally followed. Insurance can be furnished at THE COW BOY office.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton applied to insure the Custer Trail ranch property.

articles.text: W. T. Kennedy is the latest arrival to minister to the comfort of the inner man. As he carries a hatchet all the time, we can believe him when he says that he has as good goods for the money as can be bought anywhere.
articles.summary: W. T. Kennedy has opened a saloon (the 'Medora, the 1st').

articles.text: A number of good ball-players have materialized and if any town up or down the line wants a game a communication to that effect will receive a favorable answer. Several old buttons and things could be raked up that say Medora can down any local nine on the Missouri division.
articles.summary: Medora ball-players offer to play any town on the Missouri division.

articles.text: Mr. C. D. Edick, of the Bismarck firm of Edick Bros., cigar makers, has been in town for a day or two. He is much pleased with Medora's prospects and reports numerous sales of his goods. From the samples he left at THE COW BOY office, we don't blame our merchants for investing.
articles.summary: C. D. Edick of Edick Bros., Bismarck cigar makers, visited Medora.

articles.text: We sold and reserved fourteen lots last week. As this was when the public was uncertain about the freight route, we expect a large increase now that the matter is settled. We would especially urge citizens to invest at once as the lots are sure to go off rapidly and the bargains will soon be gone.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy office sold and reserved fourteen town lots last week.

articles.text: The lots on the south side of the track have been priced and are now for sale at THE COW BOY office. We don't think there is any need of booming them as they will go off very rapidly. Anyone knows, however, that it is for his interest to be among the first to buy and secure the choicest location.
articles.summary: Lots south of the track are priced and for sale at the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: Mr. Duncan, of the new Mandan furniture house of Duncan & Hilles spent Monday and Tuesday in town. He is well known all along the road and was very successful in obtaining orders. The advertisement of the firm appearing in this issue, will for the future call the attention of our citizens to the best place to buy furniture.
articles.summary: Mr. Duncan of Duncan & Hilles, Mandan furniture dealers, took orders in Medora Monday and Tuesday.

articles.text: If the person who stole the card-case from THE COW BOY office thinks it a joke, he must understand that it has lasted too long to be funny. It has been found out who took it and if it is not returned by to-morrow night, there will be some serious explaining to be done. There is no reward offered, but some very embarrassing questions will be asked unless it is returned on time.
articles.summary: A card-case stolen from the Cow Boy office; the thief is known and given until tomorrow night to return it.

articles.text: Howard Eaton will soon receive a number of registered pedigreed Holstein cattle, recently imported. The two-year-olds are worth $250 or over and altogether it will be the most valuable lot of cattle ever brought into the country. It is principally for their reception that the large barn is to be built at the Custer Trail home ranch. The Holsteins were bought by Mr. Huidakoper in Holland.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton will receive imported registered Holstein cattle, bought in Holland by Mr. Huidekoper; a large barn is to be built at the Custer Trail ranch for them.

articles.text: The Marchioness de Mores, her friend, Miss Wright, and a relative, Mr. Liebre, arrived last evening in the Marquis' private car, Montana. The party were not at all fatigued by their trip and immediately started on a tour of inspection over Medora. THE COW BOY office was examined and had ye editor not forgotten how, he would have blushed at the encomiums heaped upon it and the paper To-night, together with the Marquis, they will go on to Helena where an extended stay will be made.
articles.summary: The Marquise de Mores, Miss Wright and Mr. Liebre arrived in the Marquis' private car 'Montana' and toured Medora; with the Marquis they leave tonight for Helena.

articles.text: Messrs. G. F. Randall, of Horicon, Wis., and A. J. Rich, of Ontonagon, Mich., returned this morning to their homes. They have already sent Messrs. Roberts and Friedman to Minnesota to buy cattle and as soon as possible will put 1,000 head on the range, under the charge of Howard Eaton. Messrs. Randall and Rich are lumber men and having just closed out a big deal, are doing the most sensible thing possible—putting their money into cattle. Nor could they have chosen better hands than Howard's in which to place their investment.
articles.summary: Lumbermen G. F. Randall and A. J. Rich left for home after arranging to put 1,000 cattle on the range under Howard Eaton.

articles.text: The old timers will have to take a back seat. A tenderfoot has come to town and broken the record on rustling. He started last Sunday morning on a visit to one of Medora's suburbs. Finding a check on a seat he put it in his hat and although the conductor knew him, the tenderfoot's gall knocked him out so that he couldn't muster courage to say a word about the ticket. Arriving at his destination he reports having an elegant time, which was undoubtedly the case. Of course, it cost something so he made expenses by inveigling his host into a quiet game of draw. Having seduced a brakeman from the path of rectitude into a state of inebriety he was permitted to ride back on the bumpers of a freight train. The old timers will have to rustle a while longer to beat this.
articles.summary: Humorous item on a tenderfoot who rode free to a neighboring town on Sunday and back on a freight train.

articles.text: There are still a number of subscribers to THE COW BOY who have not paid up. To these we would say that we propose to adhere strictly to our three-months' rule. Notice will be sent to each one and if the delinquency is allowed to run a quarter, the name will be dropped and we will charge the amount to profit and loss. On general principles a subscriber who will not pay before the end of the first quarter does not mean to pay at all and the sooner we get rid of him the better. There will be some who have neglected the matter meaning to pay. A failure to receive THE COW BOY will notify these anew. No business can be run without money and printing is no exception to the rule. If anyone wants THE COW BOY they want it badly enough to pay two dollars a year.
articles.summary: Notice that subscribers in arrears a quarter will be dropped.

articles.headline: For Sale.
articles.text:
Fifteen yoke of good work steers, will be sold at reasonable rates.

HOWARD EATON, Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton offers fifteen yoke of work steers for sale.
